title: the mountain ahead
hook: the mountain ahead; the prayers Jesus himself prayed

segments.voice: Yesterday, mercy, the word Pope Francis kept saying. Your line was: start with yourself. Were you a little kinder to yourself? Today is the last day of camp one. Day twenty-one.
screen: `START WITH YOURSELF.` → `THE LAST DAY OF CAMP ONE.`

segments.voice: Look back down the hill for a second. Three weeks ago you started with grace, at a kitchen table. Then the sign of the cross. The Mass, in three scenes. Mary. The saints. Francis. Candles. The rosary: its beads, and the Hail Mary. Confession. Sunday. The Our Father. Lent. Easter. The Eucharist. The Church. Teresa. Mercy. Twenty words. That's the vocabulary: the words a Catholic hears every week. Now look up. There's a mountain ahead, and it's made of stories. But first, one more word, and it's the prayer book that Jesus himself grew up praying.
screen: `TWENTY WORDS, DOWN THE HILL.` → `THE WORDS OF EVERY WEEK.` → `A MOUNTAIN MADE OF STORIES.`

segments.voice: The Psalms are a book of one hundred and fifty songs and prayers in the middle of the Bible. The Hebrew name is Tehillim: praises. Our word psalm comes from Greek, a song sung to a plucked string. They were Israel's prayer book and hymnal, and Jesus, a Jewish boy in Nazareth, would have known many of them by heart. Here's what surprises people: they aren't all nice. Some are joyful. Some are furious. Some are people in the dark asking God where he's gone. On the cross, in Matthew's Gospel, Jesus cries out the first line of one of those, in the Douay-Rheims Bible: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" That's a psalm. Even in his worst hour he prayed with words he'd learned as a child. And in Luke, his last words are from a psalm too: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Here's a detail you'll notice if you look them up in an older Catholic Bible: the numbers are often off by one. The Douay-Rheims follows the ancient Greek and Latin numbering, so the psalm Jesus cried on the cross is Psalm 21 there, and Psalm 22 in most other Bibles. Same words, different count. Catholics still pray them every day. At every Mass there's a psalm, sung back and forth, between the readings; remember scene one. Priests, monks and nuns pray the psalms through the day in what's called the Liturgy of the Hours. The rosary was once the poor man's psalter. One hundred and fifty psalms, one for nearly every feeling a person can have. One hundred and fifty doors.
screen: `TEHILLIM — PRAISES.` · `NOT ALL OF THEM NICE.` · `MY GOD, WHY HAST THOU FORSAKEN ME?` · `THE NUMBERS ARE OFF BY ONE.` · then, large: `150 DOORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice for the end of camp one. A seventy-five-second sit. Ask yourself what you're actually feeling today, honestly. Glad. Tired. Angry. Lost. Grateful. Whatever it is, the Psalms say there's a door for it, and you don't have to clean it up first. Name the feeling in one word. Then breathe with it, not against it. If you pray, you can hand God that one word, just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The Psalms. One hundred and fifty praises, laments and songs, the prayer book Jesus himself prayed. Twenty-first word, and the last of camp one.
Your line: 150 doors. Today, if you can, open a Bible to the middle and read one psalm, any one. Tomorrow, camp two: the stories, starting with two pregnant women. Day twenty-one.

screen: `DAY 21 COUNTS.` → `CAMP ONE: DONE.` → `TOMORROW: TWO PREGNANT WOMEN.`
